entry.title: 信息流不是世界
entry.content:
EN

TL;DR —— 互联网不会把现实随机地展示给我们。任何内容出现在屏幕上之前，都已经经过了多轮选择，而这些选择会在我们把观察转化为对世界的判断之前不断叠加。每一条帖子都可能是真的，但由这些真实内容拼出来的世界，仍然可能极不具有代表性。

为什么感觉所有人都在领先

我开始不太相信“别人都过得比我好”这种感觉了。

它会根据你所在的平台变成不同的样子。在一个平台上，你会觉得所有准备考研的人都已经上岸；换一个地方，你又会觉得每个研究者都在发论文，每家创业公司都融到了钱，每个参赛者都在获奖。以个人经历为主的内容流里，普通关系甚至像是不存在，留下来的只有出轨、羞辱、冲突和怨恨。

我们通常会分别解释这些印象。考研焦虑被归结为比较，职业焦虑被归结为幸存者偏差，性别敌意被归结为极化。这些解释都不完全错，但它们共同指向了另一个问题：当一组真实却经过选择的事件，成为我们认识现实的材料时，会发生什么？

我的暂时判断很简单：到达我们面前的东西，本来就已经被筛选过了。我不想直接假定这些机制最后一定会产生同一种结果。我更想知道的是，当它们一个接一个地发生时，现实会怎样被重新组成。

最先消失的是哪些人

假设有 100 个人一起准备一场考试，其中 20 个人最终成功，80 个人没有达到自己的目标。你在网上遇到的不会是这 100 个人。成功的人有一个自然的宣布时刻：“我终于上岸了。”考得普通的人可能觉得没有什么值得分享，而失败的人也许根本不想开口。

这并不意味着成功的人都会发帖，失败的人都会消失。真正发生的是，一个人能否被看见，可能已经和结果有关。成功往往比失败更容易宣布，成就比没有完成的尝试更容易写成故事，一个已经整理好的结果也比混乱而仍在进行的过程更适合分享。

关于社交媒体参与的研究一再发现，大量用户主要是沉默的消费者，公开内容却由少数高频用户贡献。关于线上自我呈现的研究也发现，人们往往会整理出更积极、更漂亮、更成功或更理想化的自我形象。我们还没有在很多日常领域测出一条精确的选择函数，比如获奖后发帖的概率究竟是落选后的多少倍。这些概率会随着平台和场景变化，但方向已经很难忽视。

互联网一开始就已经不是一个随机的总体样本。那些没有出现的人本身也携带信息。失败的人更容易保持沉默，普通的事情更不值得发布，一次失败的实验可能只留在笔记本里，一段正常的关系也许永远不会成为故事。消失的内容并不是随机缺失的，它们往往正是因为普通、痛苦、私密，或者难以讲述，才没有进入信息流。

选择会不断叠加

推荐开始以前，还有一层筛选：什么事情值得说。一个人一年里可能经历几百件事，但最后只有少数被写成公开故事。升职、获奖、一次漂亮的旅行、一场激烈的争吵，通常都比一个普通的星期二更容易发布。接着还有活跃度的差异：有人一个月发一次，有人一天发十次。即使经历相似，高频发帖的人也会贡献更多别人能够看到的世界。

再想象两条帖子。一条说“今天复习了八个小时”，另一条说“二战之后，我终于考上了北大”。后者有更清楚的叙事、更强的情绪弧线，也更容易让人理解和回应。冲突、愤怒、惊讶、恐惧、指责和极端成功拥有同样的优势：它们更显眼。

这不代表用户真的喜欢自己互动过的所有内容。人们可能在愤怒的政治内容上停留更久，却并不希望生活里有更多愤怒；也可能只是因为一条帖子挑衅性很强才去评论，而不是因为它有用或具有代表性。但当互动被当成排序信号时，注意力优势就会变成曝光优势。一条获得更多反应的帖子，会获得更多继续获得反应的机会。

大型审计和随机信息流实验发现，以互动为基础的排序会增加愤怒、焦虑、敌意、毒性和政治冲突内容的曝光。平台不需要制造虚假信息，只要不断放大那些本来就拥有选择优势的内容即可。

在一个简单的 toy simulation 里，一个在现实总体中只占 1% 的群体，在使用互动排序后可以占到信息流的约 8%。如果这个群体的发帖活跃度又是其他人的十倍，它在信息流中的占比甚至可能接近 50%。这不是对任何具体平台的预测，而是提醒我们：可见性上的小差异，足以变成对现实频率的大误判。

每个人都住在不同的信息邻里

个性化又增加了一层选择。如果我持续阅读 AI、科研、竞赛、考研或创业内容，系统就会知道这些话题更可能留住我的注意力。它会继续把这个兴趣邻里里的人正在讨论、生产和互动的内容推给我。

我的信息流因此越来越取决于自己的历史、所在网络、兴趣，以及和我相似的人正在做什么。一个 AI 研究者打开 Twitter，会想：“为什么所有人都在做 Agent？”一个准备考研的人打开小红书，会想：“为什么所有人都上岸了？”一个创业者打开信息流，会想：“怎么大家都已经融到钱了？”

每个人都生活在一个不同的局部现实里。这并不意味着个性化必然会造成深层的意识形态极化。大型实验发现，改变人们看到的内容，确实会改变他们的曝光和对社会规范的判断，但对更持久的态度影响并不一致。个性化明确改变了观察，至于它如何改变长期信念，情况要复杂得多。

这个系统最有情绪冲击力的地方，在于那些不发帖的人。假设 100 个人参加考试，20 个人成功，80 个人失败。成功者中有很多人分享结果，失败者中的大多数却没有。信息流里出现的成功故事远多于现实总体中的成功比例，而平台又会因为这些故事能抓住注意力，把它们分发得更广。

那些失败的人随后进入一个由成功者主导的信息流，开始想：“为什么好像只有我没考上？”但屏幕另一边可能正有许多和他们一样的人，只是出于同样的原因保持沉默。大量沉默的失败者共同观看少数高度可见的成功者，每一个成功故事都可能完全真实，失真却发生在它暗示的频率上。一个人不需要相信谎言才会感到孤独，只要把一个被选择出来的样本误认为总体就够了。

信息流选择我们看到的，头脑再把它变成世界模型

信息流选择我们看到的东西，头脑则把看到的东西变成一个关于世界的模型。

人会自然地把容易回想起来的事情当作常见事情的线索。鲜明、情绪化、反复出现的内容，会显得比实际更有代表性。我们会悄悄把“我经常看到”替换成“这种事情经常发生”，即使刷到很多上岸帖并不能告诉我们真实的录取率，看到很多融资公告也不能告诉我们有多少创业公司安静地失败了。

关于社交媒体愤怒的研究发现，观察者往往会高估其他用户实际有多愤怒，而这种高估还可能扩展为对群体情绪、交流规范、敌意和极化的错误判断。更近的随机信息流实验也发现，改变排序算法能够改变人们对社会规范和群体敌意的感知。另一些实验则发现，反复看到理想化或非常成功的人，会引发向上比较，降低自我评价和幸福感。

把这些环节放在一起，过程大致可以写成：world → published world → ranked world → personalized world → remembered world → perceived world。其中的很多连接都已经被单独研究过。我们有关于参与不平等、选择性自我呈现、互动驱动的曝光、个性化信息环境、线上愤怒高估，以及反复向上比较所带来心理代价的证据。

但把它们连成完整管线的工作还不够充分。一个在现实中只占 1% 的事件，怎样变成信息流里占 8%、20% 或 50% 的内容？这种改变过的信息流，又怎样改变一个人对“什么是正常”的估计？这种估计接下来会不会改变行为和发帖？我并不是在说，已有研究已经证明了一套完整的观察失真理论。现有证据支持其中很多箭头，而把这些箭头看作同一条管线，是我目前提出的一个工作假设。

所以这里最重要的区别，不只是“真实还是虚假”，而是“具有代表性，还是被选择出来的”。那个学生确实考上了，那个研究者确实发了论文，那个创业者确实融到了钱。被遗漏的是：这些故事究竟从怎样的总体中被筛选出来。互联网不需要展示虚假信息就能误导我们，它只需要展示那些经过多次筛选、最终已经不再像原始世界的真实信息。

我们应该怎样改变

答案不是禁止情绪化内容，也不是强迫每个信息流达到完美的五五开。极端经历是真实的，人们也应该能够谈论它们。但推荐系统可以不只优化即时互动，还可以考虑持续曝光是否会让用户误解现实。目标不是删除特殊或有争议的经历，而是避免那些拥有异常注意力优势的内容被无限放大。

平台也可以提供更多关于样本如何形成的信息。系统不必只告诉我：“因为你看过 AI 内容，所以推荐这条。”它还可以告诉我：“你最近的信息流中有 25% 属于这一类内容。这是一个个性化样本，不代表它在总体中的发生率。”这不会自动消除选择偏差，却至少会让选择过程变得可见。

我们也可以养成一个小习惯。下一次看到又一个人宣布自己取得重大成就时，先问一句：“为什么我最近总能看到这些？”“我看到很多”不等于“现实中有很多”。它只说明某种选择过程产生了这次观察，而这个过程值得被重新检查。

互联网最大的危险，也许不是它给了我们虚假信息，而是它给了我们真实、却极不具有代表性的信息。一千条真实但经过选择的事实，仍然可以拼出一个不存在的世界。问题不只是我们没有看到所有人，而是那些没有被看到的人，并不是随机缺席的。信息流不是世界，它只是世界被选择之后的一次观察，而我们还在学习如何区分两者。

证据与来源

这篇文章把几组分别得到验证的研究发现放在了一条解释管线里。下面这条更完整的管线是我的综合判断，并不是说某一篇现有研究已经证明了全部过程。

  • Pew Research Center 2020 年对 10,093 名美国成年人关于线上政治与社会议题参与的调查。
  • Overperception of moral outrage in online social networks inflates beliefs about intergroup hostility，发表于 Nature Human Behaviour。
  • A meta-analysis of the effects of social media exposure to upward comparison targets on self-evaluations and emotions。
  • Out-group animosity drives engagement on social media，发表于 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences。
  • Reranking partisan animosity in algorithmic social media feeds alters affective polarization，发表于 Science。

entry.title: The Feed Is Not the World

link.title: The Feed Is Not the World

entry.content:
中文

TL;DR — The internet does not show us a random sample of reality. What reaches us has already been selected, and the selection compounds before the mind turns observation into a belief about the world. Every post may be true, yet the world assembled from those truths can still be deeply unrepresentative.

The feeling that everyone else is ahead

I have started to distrust the feeling that everyone else is doing better.

It appears in different forms depending on where I look. On one platform, it is the feeling that everyone preparing for a graduate entrance exam has been admitted. Somewhere else, it becomes the impression that every researcher is publishing papers, every startup is raising money, and every competitor is winning prizes. On platforms built around personal stories, it can feel as if ordinary relationships barely exist anymore, only betrayal, humiliation, conflict, and resentment.

We usually explain these impressions one at a time. Exam anxiety becomes comparison. Career anxiety becomes survivorship bias. Gender hostility becomes polarization. None of those explanations is completely wrong, but taken together they point to a broader question: what happens when a collection of true but selected events becomes the material from which we construct a picture of reality?

My working hypothesis is simple. What reaches us has already been selected. Some people speak more readily than others, some experiences are easier to display, and some kinds of content travel farther once they enter a platform. I do not want to assume that these mechanisms always produce the same outcome. I want to understand what happens when they operate in sequence.

The people who disappear first

Imagine 100 people preparing for an exam. Perhaps 20 of them eventually succeed, while 80 do not reach the outcome they wanted. You will never encounter all 100 of them online. The successful student has an obvious announcement, “I finally got in,” while someone with an ordinary result may feel that there is little worth sharing. A person who failed may not want to say anything at all.

This does not mean that every successful person posts or that every unsuccessful person disappears. It means that the probability of becoming visible may already depend on what happened. A success is often easier to announce than a failure. An achievement is easier to turn into a story than an unfinished attempt. A polished outcome is easier to share than a confusing process that is still underway.

Research on social-media participation consistently finds that a large share of users are mostly silent consumers, while a small minority produces a disproportionate amount of public content. Research on self-presentation also finds that people tend to curate more positive, attractive, successful, or idealized versions of their lives. We still do not have a clean estimate for many everyday selection functions, such as how much more likely someone is to post after winning a competition than after losing one. Those probabilities vary by platform and context, but the direction is difficult to ignore.

The internet begins with a population that is already missing people in a non-random way. People who fail may be more likely to remain silent. Ordinary events may be less likely to be published. An unsuccessful experiment may stay in a notebook. A normal relationship may never become a story. The things missing from the feed are not random omissions; they disappear partly because they are ordinary, painful, private, or difficult to narrate.

Selection compounds

There is another filter before recommendation begins: what feels worth saying. A person may live through hundreds of events in a year, but only a few become public stories. A promotion, a prize, a beautiful trip, a dramatic argument, or an unusually difficult experience is easier to publish than a normal Tuesday. Some people then post once a month, while others post ten times a day. Even among people with similar lives, the most active users contribute far more of the world that everyone else can see.

Consider two posts. One says, “I studied for eight hours today.” The other says, “After failing twice, I finally got into Peking University.” The second post has a stronger narrative, a clearer emotional arc, and a more visible outcome. It is easier to understand and easier to react to. Conflict, outrage, surprise, fear, accusation, and extreme success have the same advantage: they are salient.

This does not mean that users genuinely prefer everything they engage with. People may spend more time on angry political content without wanting more anger in their lives. They may comment because something is provocative, not because it is useful or representative. But when engagement becomes a ranking signal, attention advantage can become exposure advantage. A post that receives more reactions is given more opportunities to receive reactions.

Large audits and randomized feed experiments have found that engagement-oriented ranking can increase exposure to anger, anxiety, hostility, toxicity, and political conflict. The platform does not need to fabricate anything. It only needs to repeatedly amplify content that already has a selection advantage.

In a simple toy simulation, a group that represents only 1% of the underlying population can become roughly 8% of the feed under engagement-based ranking. If that group also posts ten times more actively than everyone else, its feed share can approach 50%. That is not a forecast of any particular platform. It is a reminder that small differences in visibility can become large differences in perceived reality.

Everyone lives in a different neighborhood

Personalization adds another layer. If I spend my time reading about AI, research, competitions, graduate school, or startups, the system learns that these topics are likely to hold my attention. It begins showing me more of what people in that interest neighborhood are discussing, producing, and reacting to.

My feed becomes increasingly conditioned on my history, my network, my interests, and the behavior of people similar to me. An AI researcher opens Twitter and wonders why everyone is building agents. A student preparing for an exam opens Xiaohongshu and wonders why everyone is getting admitted. A founder checks their feed and wonders how everyone has already raised money.

Each person is living inside a different local reality. This does not mean that personalization automatically produces deep ideological polarization. Large experiments have found that changing what people see can alter their exposure and their perception of social norms, while having mixed effects on more durable attitudes. Personalization clearly changes observation; its consequences for long-term belief are more complicated.

The emotional force of the system becomes clearest when we consider people who do not post. Suppose 100 people take an exam. Twenty succeed and 80 fail. Many of the successful students share their results. Most of the unsuccessful students do not. The feed now contains far more success stories than the underlying population does, and the platform distributes those stories because they attract attention.

The people who failed then encounter a stream dominated by the people who succeeded. They begin to think, “How did everyone else make it?” Many people like them may be on the other side of the screen, silently watching for exactly the same reason. A large number of silent failures are collectively consuming a small number of highly visible successes. Each success story may be completely real; the distortion lies in the implied frequency.

The feed selects; the mind builds a model

The feed selects what we see. The mind turns what we see into a model of the world.

Humans naturally use what is easy to recall as a clue about what is common. Vivid, emotional, and repeatedly encountered information can feel more representative than it really is. We quietly substitute “I see this often” for “this happens often,” even though seeing many admitted students tells us nothing about the admission rate, just as seeing many founders announce funding tells us nothing about how many startups failed quietly.

Research on social-media outrage has shown that observers tend to overestimate how angry other users actually are, and that this error can expand into mistaken beliefs about collective emotion, communication norms, hostility, and polarization. More recent randomized feed research has also shown that changing ranking algorithms can alter people’s perception of social norms and group animosity. Other experiments have found that repeatedly seeing idealized or highly successful people can produce upward social comparison, lowering self-evaluation and well-being.

Put together, the process looks something like this: world → published world → ranked world → personalized world → remembered world → perceived world. Several links in this chain have been studied directly. We have evidence for unequal participation, selective self-presentation, engagement-based exposure, personalized information environments, overestimation of online outrage, and the psychological cost of repeated upward comparison.

What has not been established as clearly is the complete pipeline connecting them. How does an event that occurs in 1% of the population become 8%, 20%, or 50% of a feed? How does that altered feed change a person’s estimate of what is normal? How does that estimate influence later behavior and future posting? I am not claiming that existing research has already proved one unified theory of observation distortion. The existing evidence supports many of the links. The broader pipeline is a hypothesis about what happens when those links operate together.

That is why the important distinction is not simply true versus false, but representative versus selected. The successful student really did get admitted, the researcher really did publish, and the founder really did raise money. The missing context is the population from which those stories were selected. The internet can mislead us without showing us false information; it can show us true information that has been filtered so many times that the final composition no longer resembles the world it came from.

What should change?

The answer is not to ban emotional content or force every feed into a perfect 50/50 balance. Extreme experiences are real, and people should be allowed to talk about them. Recommendation systems could still optimize for utility while accounting for whether repeated exposure is likely to distort a user’s understanding of the world. The aim would be to stop content with unusually strong attention advantages from being amplified without limit, not to remove unusual or controversial experiences.

Platforms could also provide more information about how a sample was formed. Instead of only saying, “You are seeing this because you watched AI content,” a system might say, “Twenty-five percent of your recent feed belongs to this category. This is a personalized sample and does not represent its prevalence in the wider population.” That would not remove selection bias, but it would make the selection visible.

We can develop a similar habit ourselves. When we see another announcement of a major achievement, we can ask why we are seeing so many of them before drawing a conclusion. I saw many does not mean there are many. It means that some process produced this observation, and that process may be worth examining.

The internet’s greatest danger may not be that it gives us false information. It may be that it gives us information that is true, but profoundly unrepresentative. A thousand true, carefully selected facts can still assemble a world that does not exist. The problem is not that we failed to see everyone. The problem is that the people we did not see were not missing at random. The feed is not the world. It is a selected observation of the world, and our minds are still learning how to tell the difference.

Evidence and sources

The argument in this essay combines findings that have been tested separately. The broader pipeline is a synthesis, not a claim that one existing study has already proved the entire chain.

  • Pew Research Center’s 2020 survey of 10,093 U.S. adults on participation in political and social discussions online.
  • Overperception of moral outrage in online social networks inflates beliefs about intergroup hostility, Nature Human Behaviour.
  • A meta-analysis of the effects of social media exposure to upward comparison targets on self-evaluations and emotions.
  • Out-group animosity drives engagement on social media, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
  • Reranking partisan animosity in algorithmic social media feeds alters affective polarization, Science.

entry.title: 没有你的历史，AI 就不可能真正懂你

link.title: 没有你的历史，AI 就不可能真正懂你

entry.content:
EN

TL;DR — 大模型懂的是一般意义上的人。要让 AI 理解并真正帮助某个具体的人，它必须拥有这个人长期、可追溯、由本人控制的经历证据。数据收集不是理解本身，更不意味着无限监控；但没有这些证据，所谓 Personal AI 只能是一个很会给通用建议的陌生人。

现在的 AI 总是太早开始帮助人。聊不了几句，它已经可以告诉你怎样睡得更好、如何保持专注、应该学习什么、怎样规划职业。那些建议可能完全正确，表达得也足够体贴。可在这份流畅背后，AI 对接受建议的人依然所知甚少。它不知道你曾经试过哪些方法，不知道那些尝试为什么失败，也不知道某个对大多数人有效的策略，为什么到了你这里总是只能维持两个星期。

这正是今天许多 “Personal AI” 的矛盾：交互界面是个人化的，知识却仍然是通用的。系统会叫你的名字，记得你喜欢怎样的回答，也能模仿适合你的语气，但它对你的判断大多临时拼接自当前这段对话。它可能很懂心理学、教育和人类行为，却不知道这些一般规律在你身上会怎样组合，哪些成立，哪些失效，哪些甚至恰好相反。

如果 AI 真想理解并帮助一个具体的人，数据收集就不能只是产品边缘的一项可选功能。它是整个主张的证据基础。一个系统在说“我知道你是怎样运作的”之前，至少应该见过你在真实时间里怎样生活、学习、选择、失败和改变。

模型懂“人”，不等于懂你

能力很强的 Foundation Model 拥有关于人的巨大知识。它读过行为研究、人物传记、医学资料、教育实践和大量对话，知道人在不同情境下通常会有什么反应，也知道哪些干预在统计意义上更可能有效。借用一个简单的 Bayesian 视角，它掌握的是非常丰富的先验：P(human)。

Personal AI 面对的却是另一个问题：当这个人的经历、环境、关系、选择和失败都已经发生之后，他现在最可能怎样思考，又会怎样变化？这里需要的是 P(you | your history)。前者给出“对人来说通常合理”的答案，后者才有机会给出“对你来说有依据”的帮助。这不是换一种推荐算法，而是两个不同的认识对象。

模型再强，也无法凭能力本身补回一段从未见过的历史。更好的模型可以从更少的证据里看出更多东西，可以识别更细的模式，也可以更谨慎地处理不确定性；但它不能凭空知道你过去十年经历了什么。模型能力决定系统能从证据中学到多少，个人历史决定它学到的究竟是谁。

所以通用建议才会如此容易出现：多睡觉、多运动、设定目标、减少干扰、坚持练习。它们之所以常见，是因为对很多人都有用。可“普遍有用”和“适合这个人”不是一回事。真正需要回答的是：什么形式的运动是你能长期坚持的，它在什么环境下会发生，过去几次为什么中断，它又怎样影响你的情绪与认知。没有历史，这些问题只能靠猜。

上下文窗口装不下一生

也许有人会说，只要和 AI 多聊一会儿，把过去完整讲给它听，不就能建立理解了吗？对话当然重要，但自我叙述只是一种证据。人会遗忘，会压缩经历，也会在事后为自己的行为寻找更连贯的解释。今天觉得重要的事情，可能遮住半年前真正改变方向的细节。我们可能真诚地相信自己具有某个模式，行为记录却并不支持；也可能完全没有察觉一个已经重复出现很多次的规律。

当前对话能呈现的是一张快照：你此刻说得出的目标、此刻记得的事实，以及此刻的情绪。理解一个人却必须看见变化。什么变了，什么始终没变，哪些问题离开后又不断回来，哪些看似稳定的模式在环境变化后立刻消失？这些都是时间问题，再长的一次对话也无法替代纵向证据。

静态 Profile 同样不够。一个 profile.json 可以保存职业、兴趣、沟通偏好和主动声明的目标，这些信息很有用，但它仍然没有解释一个人怎样运作。知道某个人喜欢数学，不等于知道他怎样学会数学、为什么会放弃某类教材、形式化语言在什么时候阻碍理解，又是什么真实问题让他愿意熬过困难。

Personal AI 需要的因此不只是“记得一些事实”，而是一份可以重新检查的经历记录：发生了什么，当时处在怎样的情境里，这个人似乎想解决什么，后来出现了什么结果，新证据又怎样改变了我们对那次经历的理解。这不是把 Prompt 做得更长，而是要建立一层新的基础设施。

收集不等于理解，但理解必须从收集开始

理解一个人的第一层，只是知道发生过什么。他读了什么、写了什么、构建了什么，哪些事情被一再推迟，哪些项目完成了，哪些在最初的兴奋过去后被放弃；当状态特别好或特别差时，他在哪里、睡眠如何、使用什么工具、前后发生过哪些变化。数字行为、身体状态、主动反思和现实结果，分别照亮个人轨迹的不同部分。

这些观察单独拿出来几乎都不能说明什么。读完七篇论文，不代表真正学到了东西；在编辑器里待十个小时，也不等于完成了有效工作；睡眠不足可能导致注意力下降，也可能只是同时发生。Raw Trace 是证据，不是结论。收集的作用不是抢先宣布数据意味着什么，而是保留足够多的现实，让之后的解释可以被验证，而不是被编造出来。

接下来才是 Experience Reconstruction。分散的事件要重新放回它们所属的问题、意图和变化过程里。“读了七篇论文”可能被还原为：“为了理解评估为何逐渐偏离 latent goal，他把注意力从模型结构转向验证机制，并排除了两个原本看似合理的解释。”到了这里，系统不再只是在统计活动，而是在重建这个人试图理解什么，以及他的认知表示如何发生变化。

再往上，系统才有机会发现一个人跨时间的工作方式。什么问题会让他持续进入深度探索？哪一种反馈真的改变行为，而不是只换来一句认同？为什么有些项目能穿过新鲜感继续生长，另一些却总在进入重复执行后消失？哪些兴趣只是短期 novelty，哪些问题几年后仍然回来？这些并不是传感器可以直接采到的事实，而是足够多的经历被保存和重建之后，才有资格提出的假设。

顺序不能颠倒：Trace → Experience → Representation → Pattern → Human Model。跳过前面的层次，并不会让系统显得更聪明，只会让后面的判断失去依据。如果 AI 根据几次零散行为就断言“你就是这样的人”，那不是理解，而是在用不足的证据讲一个听起来很完整的故事。

Human Model 应该像科学模型一样工作

收集个人数据，不是为了建立一座事无巨细的人生档案馆，而是为了支持一个持续更新的 Human Model。它保存的是关于这个人的目标、知识、策略、优势、瓶颈、环境和变化规律的一组暂时判断。它不应该声称终于发现了“真实的你”。人不是等待分类的静态对象，有些旧模式甚至会因为被看见而开始改变。

一个可靠的 Human Model 应该更像科学模型，而不是性格测试。每个判断都有不确定性，每次推断都能回到产生它的证据，后续观察也能够加强、缩小或推翻原来的结论。系统必须分清哪些是本人明确说过的事实，哪些是根据行为作出的推断；也要分清一个跨半年反复出现的模式，与最近一次偶然的异常。

Provenance 让这种修正成为可能。如果 AI 认为某个人总会在项目从探索进入重复执行后失去动力，他应该能看到这个判断从哪里来：三次最近的中断、过去半年的共同模式、一段自我陈述，还是模型套用了一个常见的人群印象？系统考虑过哪些其他解释？什么样的新证据会让它改变想法？如果这些连接不存在，“理解你”就会变成一种无法质疑的权威。

纵向数据也让理解第一次变得可以检验。昨天形成的模型，要接受明天行为的验证；系统认为某种环境能改善持续注意力，结果就应该能够被观察；提出一个干预后，也要继续测量行为有没有改变、结果是否改善、改变能否保持。Observe、Model、Intervene、Measure、Update 形成闭环之后，个人理解才不再是一场语言表演，而是一个会失败、会学习、也会修正自己的过程。

有了这些证据，帮助才可能真正属于你

建立这套基础设施，不是为了知道得更多，而是为了让帮助更准确。有效的发展至少需要三个要素：这个人当前处在什么状态，他自己希望抵达什么状态，以及从这里走向那里时，什么变化机制真的会起作用。通用建议往往只说出了目标，却没有处理另外两项。

例如，一个人希望提升数学能力。通用系统会推荐教材、习题和学习计划；基于个人历史的系统则可能发现，他能很快形成关于 Optimization 的直觉，也擅长跨领域迁移抽象结构，但当形式语言脱离真实问题单独出现时，理解就会受阻。过去的记录还表明，孤立的课程经常被放弃，从正在研究的问题反向补齐数学时，知识却更容易保留下来。合适的干预不再是“多学数学”，而是围绕这个人真正能维持注意力、并把直觉转成形式理解的机制重新设计学习。

干预发生后，收集仍然不能停止。新的环境有没有改变行为？形式化能力真的提高了，还是投入时间变多了？这种提高能否迁移到新的问题？真正有效的是内容、时机、社交情境，还是某个尚未被记录的身体变化？结果会成为下一轮证据。帮助一个人与继续理解这个人，从此变成同一个循环的两面。

这也是长期数据与普通个性化设置最不同的地方。设置改变的是系统怎样呈现信息，历史让系统逐渐学习这个人怎样发生变化。当这种变化规律变得更清楚，AI 才可能越过“重复正确建议”这一步，开始帮助设计更适合个人的环境、任务、反馈和外部支持。

论证收集的必要，也必须论证它的边界

Personal AI 需要数据，不等于它应该收集一切。无差别采集可能带来的不是理解，而是噪声、风险和权力。这里的数据不是与主体无关的训练语料，而是一个真实的人留下的生活轨迹：敏感、具体、不完整，也无法和经历它的人分开。系统越敢对这个人作出强判断，这个人对数据和判断的控制权就必须越强。

因此，个人数据基础设施应该尽可能 local-first，默认由用户所有，并按来源和用途授权，同时明确保存期限。人应该能够检查系统收集了什么，纠正错误记录，删除或导出数据，也应该知道哪些上层判断依赖这些证据。当底层记录被删除或证明有误时，系统必须找出哪些结论需要重新评估。Provenance 不只用于工程调试，它让人有能力反驳系统为自己写下的解释。

收集与解释也必须分开。发生过什么，不自动等于为什么发生；一个推断出的 Representation 不是已经验证的事实；反复出现的 Pattern 更不是一个人的永久身份。保持这些层次的边界，可以避免暂时行为过早凝固成标签，也允许不同解释围绕同一组证据竞争。

正确的原则从来不是“尽可能多地收集”，而是：在本人授权下，保存足够且相关的证据，让关于这个人的判断可以追溯，让对这个人的帮助可以检验。 衡量标准不是数据量，而是系统能不能说清楚自己知道什么、怀疑什么、依据来自哪里，以及这个人怎样质疑或撤回它。

没有历史，就没有 Personal AI

模型训练让整个 AI 领域明白了一件事：能力不会只从架构里自然长出来，它需要数据。Personal Intelligence 也面对一项类似的要求。Foundation Model 通过通用数据获得能力，个人系统通过关于一个人的纵向证据，才逐渐变得真正 personal。这些数据不必进入全局模型训练，它们可以保持私有、本地并由本人控制，只在检索、经历重建、推断和持续更新中发挥作用。

缺少这一层，所谓 Personal AI 仍然只是一个拥有丰富知识的陌生人。它可以说得温暖，记住你偏好的格式，也可能给出有用建议，却无法稳定地区分“什么通常对人有益”和“什么确实对你有效”。它不知道你怎样成为现在的自己，也无法检验什么真正帮助你改变，更不知道自己对你的判断从什么时候开始已经过时。

如果我们希望 AI 理解人，就必须让它能够从人的真实经历中学习；如果希望它帮助某一个具体的人，这些经历就必须跨越时间、保留来源、允许检查，并由经历它的人拥有。Data Collection 不是终点，单靠数据也永远不会自动产生理解。但任何系统只要认真声称自己足够理解一个人、能够帮助一个人，脚下都必须先有这层证据。

没有你的历史，AI 就不可能真正懂你。
entry.summary: 为什么长期、可追溯的个人数据，是 AI 理解并真正帮助一个具体的人所必需的基础。

entry.title: No History, No Personal AI
entry.content:
中文

TL;DR — A foundation model can understand humans in general, but it cannot understand a particular person without evidence from that person’s life. Longitudinal data collection is not the same as understanding, yet without it, personal understanding is impossible. If we want AI to help a human in ways that are genuinely for them, we first need a user-owned, traceable record of how that person actually lives, learns, changes, and grows.

Most AI systems begin helping too early. After a few messages, they are already prepared to tell you how to sleep better, stay focused, learn faster, choose a career, or become more disciplined. The advice may be sensible. It may even be delivered with remarkable empathy. But beneath the fluency, the system still knows very little about the person receiving it. It does not know which advice you have already tried, what happened when you tried it, why a strategy that works for others repeatedly fails for you, or what kind of change has actually lasted in your life.

This is the central problem with most “personal” AI today: it is personal in interface, but generic in knowledge. It speaks to you, remembers a few stated preferences, and adapts its tone, yet its model of you is mostly reconstructed from the current conversation. The system may know a great deal about psychology, learning, health, and human behavior. What it does not know is how those general patterns combine in this particular human.

If AI is ever going to understand and genuinely help an individual, data collection cannot remain an optional feature at the edge of the product. It is the epistemic foundation of the entire claim. Before a system can say, “I understand how you work,” it needs evidence of how you have actually worked across time.

A model can know humans without knowing you

A powerful foundation model contains an extraordinary amount of knowledge about people. It has learned from descriptions of human behavior, scientific research, biographies, conversations, medical literature, educational practice, and countless examples of how people respond to different situations. In Bayesian terms, it has a rich prior: P(human). It knows what people tend to do, which interventions often work, and which explanations are plausible across a population.

Personal intelligence asks for something else. It asks for P(you | your history): an understanding of this person after accounting for the events, environments, choices, failures, relationships, and changes that have shaped them. The difference between those two distributions is not a small product improvement. It is the difference between advice that is statistically reasonable and help that is grounded in the reality of one life.

Model capability cannot remove this gap. A more capable model may infer more from less evidence, detect subtler patterns, and reason more carefully about uncertainty. But it cannot recover a history it has never observed. Intelligence determines how much a system can learn from evidence; it does not create the missing evidence. Without longitudinal personal data, even the strongest model is forced to fill the gaps with population-level assumptions.

That is why generic advice appears so quickly. “Sleep more.” “Exercise.” “Set clear goals.” “Reduce distractions.” “Practice consistently.” These recommendations survive because they are broadly useful. But broad usefulness is not the same as personal relevance. The question is not whether exercise is generally good. The question is what form of exercise this person can sustain, under which conditions, how it affects their cognition and mood, and what has caused previous attempts to disappear after two weeks. Answering that question requires a history.

A context window is not a life

It is tempting to think that a long conversation solves the problem. If the user explains enough, perhaps the model can build an accurate picture on demand. Conversation is valuable, but self-report is only one channel of evidence. People forget, compress, rationalize, and reinterpret their own past. What feels important today may crowd out what was important six months ago. A person can sincerely describe a pattern that is not visible in their behavior, or fail to notice a pattern that becomes obvious across repeated events.

Current context also has no natural sense of development. It presents a snapshot: the goals the user can articulate now, the facts they remember now, and the emotional state from which they are speaking now. But understanding a person means knowing what changed, what remained stable, what repeatedly returned, and which apparent patterns vanished when the environment changed. Those are longitudinal questions. They cannot be answered from a snapshot, however detailed the snapshot may be.

A user profile does not solve this either. A profile.json can store an occupation, a list of interests, communication preferences, declared goals, and perhaps a few durable facts. That information is useful, but it is not a model of how a person works. Knowing that someone is interested in mathematics tells us little about how they learn mathematics, why they abandon certain materials, when formal notation blocks understanding, or which real problems make them willing to persist through difficulty.

Personal AI therefore needs more than memory in the narrow sense of remembering facts. It needs a reconstructable account of experience: what happened, in what context, what the person appeared to be trying to do, what outcome followed, and how later evidence changed the meaning of the event. This is not a larger prompt. It is an infrastructure problem.

Collection is not understanding—but understanding begins with collection

The first layer of personal understanding is simply knowing what happened. What did the person read, write, build, discuss, revisit, postpone, complete, or abandon? Where were they? How did they sleep? Which tools did they use? What changed before and after a period of unusually strong or unusually weak performance? Digital activity, physical state, explicit reflection, and real-world outcomes can each reveal a different part of the trajectory.

None of these observations is meaningful by itself. Reading seven papers does not tell us whether someone learned anything. Spending ten hours in an editor does not prove that useful work happened. A week of poor sleep may explain a change in attention, or it may merely coincide with it. Raw traces are evidence, not conclusions. The role of collection is not to declare what the data means, but to preserve enough reality that meaning can later be tested rather than invented.

The second layer is experience reconstruction. Separate events must be organized around the problems, intentions, and transitions they belong to. “Read seven papers” may become “tried to understand why evaluation drifts away from a latent goal, moved from model architecture to verification, and rejected two previously plausible explanations.” The system is no longer counting activity. It is reconstructing what the person was attempting to understand and how their representation of the problem changed.

The third layer is discovering how the person works across time. What kinds of problems repeatedly produce deep engagement? Which feedback changes behavior rather than merely producing agreement? Why do certain projects survive the initial excitement while others disappear? Which interests are temporary novelty, and which questions continue resurfacing for years? What environment allows the person to do their best work? These are not facts the system can collect directly. They are hypotheses that become possible only after enough experience has been collected and reconstructed.

The sequence matters: trace, experience, representation, pattern, model. Skipping the earlier layers does not make the system more intelligent. It makes the later claims less accountable. If a system jumps directly from a few observations to “this is the kind of person you are,” it is not understanding a human. It is producing a persuasive story with insufficient evidence.

A Human Model should behave like a scientific model

The goal of personal data collection is not to assemble a perfect archive of a life. It is to support a Human Model: an evolving set of beliefs about the person’s goals, knowledge, strategies, strengths, bottlenecks, environments, and patterns of change. This model should never present itself as a final description of the “true person.” Humans are not static objects waiting to be classified. They change, and sometimes they change precisely because an old pattern has been recognized.

A useful Human Model should behave more like a scientific model than a personality profile. Every claim should carry uncertainty. Every inference should be connected to the evidence that produced it. New observations should be able to strengthen, narrow, or overturn an earlier belief. The system should distinguish what the person explicitly said from what it inferred, and distinguish a recurring pattern from a recent anomaly.

Provenance is what makes this possible. If an AI believes that someone loses momentum when a project moves from exploration to repetitive execution, the person should be able to inspect why. Was the belief derived from three recent abandoned projects, a six-month pattern, a self-report, or a guess generated from a population stereotype? Were competing explanations considered? What evidence would cause the system to revise the claim? Without those links, “understanding” becomes an authority that cannot be questioned.

Longitudinal data also makes understanding measurable. A model formed yesterday can be tested against what happens tomorrow. If the system predicts that a particular environment will improve sustained attention, the outcome can be observed. If it recommends an intervention, the system can measure whether behavior changed, whether the outcome improved, and whether the improvement persisted. The loop becomes: observe, model, intervene, measure, update. Personal understanding stops being a performance and becomes a process that can fail, learn, and improve.

Better data makes better help possible

The reason to build this infrastructure is not to know a person for the sake of knowing them. It is to make help more relevant. Effective development requires at least three things: a model of the person’s current state, a desired state chosen by that person, and some understanding of the transition dynamics between them. Generic advice usually names the desired state while ignoring the other two.

Consider someone who wants to become stronger in mathematics. A generic system can recommend textbooks, exercises, and a study schedule. A system grounded in personal history might discover something more specific: the person forms strong intuitions around optimization, transfers abstractions quickly across domains, but struggles when formal language is introduced without a live problem. It may also observe that isolated courses are repeatedly abandoned, while mathematics learned backward from an active research question is retained. The appropriate intervention is no longer “study more mathematics.” It is to design learning around the mechanism by which this person actually sustains attention and converts intuition into formal understanding.

After the intervention, collection remains necessary. Did the new environment change behavior? Did formal fluency improve, or did the person simply spend more time? Did the improvement transfer to a new problem? Was the intervention effective because of the content, the timing, the social context, or some unobserved change in health? Each outcome becomes new evidence. Helping the person and understanding the person become part of the same loop.

This is what makes longitudinal data qualitatively different from personalization settings. Settings adapt the system’s presentation. History allows the system to learn the person’s change dynamics. Once those dynamics become clearer, AI can do more than repeat good advice. It can help design environments, tasks, feedback, and external supports that are responsive to how this individual actually develops.

The case for collection is also a case for restraint

Arguing that personal AI requires data does not imply that it should collect everything. Indiscriminate collection can create noise instead of understanding, and power instead of help. The data involved is not an abstract training corpus. It is the trace of a real life: sensitive, contextual, incomplete, and inseparable from the person whose experience produced it. The stronger the system’s claims about the person become, the stronger that person’s control must become as well.

Personal data infrastructure should therefore be local-first where possible, user-owned by default, permissioned by source and purpose, and explicit about retention. People should be able to inspect what was captured, correct false records, remove data, export it, and understand which derived beliefs depend on it. If underlying evidence is deleted or invalidated, the system must be able to identify which conclusions need to be reconsidered. Provenance is not only a technical feature; it is what gives the person the ability to contest the system’s account of them.

Collection should also remain separate from interpretation. A record of what happened is not automatically a judgment about why it happened. An inferred representation is not a verified fact. A pattern is not an identity. Keeping these layers distinct prevents temporary behavior from hardening into permanent labels and allows different interpretations to compete over the same evidence.

The right principle is not “collect as much as possible.” It is: collect enough of the right evidence, with the person’s authorization, to make personal claims traceable and personal help testable. The standard is not data volume. It is whether the system can explain what it knows, what it only suspects, where that belief came from, and how the person can challenge it.

No history, no personal AI

Model training taught the AI field a simple lesson: intelligence does not emerge from architecture alone. It depends on data. Personal intelligence has an analogous requirement. A foundation model becomes capable through general data; a personal system becomes personal through longitudinal evidence about the individual it serves. This evidence does not necessarily need to train the global model. It can remain private, local, and under the person’s control while supporting retrieval, reconstruction, inference, and continuous model updates.

Without that layer, a “personal AI” is still a stranger with excellent general knowledge. It may speak warmly, remember your preferred format, and offer useful suggestions, but it cannot reliably distinguish what is good for people from what is good for you. It cannot explain how you became who you are, test what helps you change, or know when its assumptions about you have stopped being true.

If we want AI to understand humans, we must give it a way to learn from human experience. If we want it to help a particular human, that experience must be longitudinal, attributable, inspectable, and owned by the person who lived it. Data collection is not the final goal, and it is never sufficient by itself. But it is the ground beneath every serious claim that a system understands a person well enough to help.

No history, no personal AI.
entry.summary: Why longitudinal personal data is the necessary foundation for AI that claims to understand—and genuinely help—an individual.

entry.title: 关系不是起点
entry.content:
EN

TL;DR — 有价值的关系很少始于主动索取连接，它们通常从共同的问题、可验证的作品和一次次靠谱的协作中长出来。先把能力变成证据，再把价值送到真正需要它的人面前；当别人知道你擅长什么、在什么事情上值得信任，关系、合作和机会才会自然发生。

我最近越来越不相信“多认识一些厉害的人”这类建议。不是因为认识人没有用，而是因为这句话太容易让人把顺序搞反：先找到一个想接近的人，再临时想一个接近他的理由。于是我们在会议结束后匆忙加微信，给研究者发一段“久仰大名，希望有机会合作”，或者在自己还没真正做出什么之前，就开始盘算怎样进入某个圈子。这些动作看起来很积极，实际上提供的信息很少。对方依然不知道你在意什么、能解决什么、思考到了哪里，也不知道为什么下一次应该再来找你。

这类交流最根本的问题，不是表达得不够漂亮，而是关系请求跑在了价值证据前面。我们希望对方先给出注意力、信任甚至机会，然后再慢慢发现我们的潜力；可站在对方的位置，他能看到的只是一个尚未被验证的自我描述。你说自己懂 Agent、懂 Benchmark、擅长研究，这些话也许都是真的，但它们仍然只存在于你的脑子里。一个陌生人没有足够的信息判断它们，更没有理由替你承担验证成本。

所以我现在更愿意相信另一种路径：不要先从关系出发，先从一件真实的事情出发。找一个你愿意长期追问的问题，做一项经得起检查的工作，提出一个能够被证伪的判断，或者造出一个确实有人需要的工具。关系不必被预先设计，它会在共同面对现实、交换证据和推动问题的过程中慢慢出现。

先有共同现实，才有连接

假设两个人都在研究长周期 Agent。一个人认为核心瓶颈是记忆，另一个人认为真正的问题在评估。两人的观点并不一致，但这种分歧反而给交流提供了扎实的结构：他们可以比较证据，追问各自假设的边界，讨论什么实验能够区分两种解释。对话不需要靠寒暄硬撑，因为问题本身会不断产生新的内容。此时，关系的起点不再是“我想认识你”，而是“我们都想弄清楚这件事”。

很多真正有生命力的研究共同体就是这样形成的。人们并不是先决定成为朋友，再寻找一个可以合作的方向；他们是在一次次撞上同一个难题时认出了彼此。做相邻工具的人开始交换方法，对同一现象持不同解释的人开始争论，某个人公开的一次失败又替其他人排除了一条错误路线。大家未必一开始就互相信任，但他们共享了一个坐标系，知道彼此的话是在回应哪一部分现实。

这也是为什么我越来越觉得，好的关系不是靠彼此注视建立的，而是靠一起看向同一个方向建立的。两个人之间不需要凭空制造内容，外部世界已经给了他们一件值得共同处理的事。关系由此不再是一项独立于工作的“社交任务”，而成了多人认真投入同一问题后自然产生的协调需求。

当然，这并不意味着所有交往都要计算产出，也不意味着友谊、好奇和善意必须先通过某种商业审查。真正应该警惕的是那种被制造出来的 networking：没有共同对象，没有真实内容，只因为对方似乎拥有资源，就急着让自己出现在他的联系人里。与其反复琢磨“我怎样才能认识这个人”，不如先问：“我在做什么事情，能让我们有一个自然、具体而且彼此都感兴趣的理由开始说话？”

先让能力变得可见

能力在留下证据之前，几乎都是不可见的。你可以相信自己很有潜力，也可以相信自己对某个领域有很深的理解，但别人无法直接读取这些东西。别人真正能够观察到的，是你写出的代码、跑过的实验、发现的失败模式、提交的 Pull Request、整理的数据集，以及你在一个方案失效后如何重新判断问题。潜力是一种私人感受，作品才是公共证据。

一个仓库、一篇分析、一套 Benchmark，甚至一个诚实而清晰的负面结果，意义都不只是“完成了一份内容”。它们在把原本潜藏的能力变得可检查。别人可以顺着作品看到你注意到了什么、忽略了什么，能不能区分猜测和结论，是否愿意把事情做完，以及当现实与预期不一致时，你会修正模型还是掩盖问题。作品越多，这个关于你的模型就越清楚。

信任也是这样积累的。它并不来自你如何有力地描述自己，而来自别人一次次获得新的证据：这个人说会做的事情真的做了；遇到问题时没有消失；表达不确定性时足够诚实；拿到一点帮助后能够继续把事情推进。每一次靠谱的输出都在降低别人理解你的成本，也在提高下一次合作发生的可能性。

这就是为什么，花十个小时做出一个真正有意思的东西，往往比花十个小时想办法“认识人”更有社交价值。好的作品不会只替你证明能力，它还会改变交流的起点。你不再是空手走到别人面前，请他相信你以后可能有价值；你带着已经发生的进展、已经暴露的问题和可以共同检查的证据进入谈话。对方不必想象你会不会做事，他可以直接看见你是怎样做事的。

做到足够深，再寻求杠杆

先独立推进，也会显著改变求助的质量。如果你一开始就问一位专家“这个研究方向应该怎么做”，听起来是在请教，实际上却把大部分认知负担交给了对方：他要替你界定问题、梳理文献、生成假设，还要判断下一步应该做什么。问题越空，对方需要投入的工作越多；而在你还没有展示执行能力时，他也不知道自己的投入是否会被真正放大。

另一种情况是，你已经读过相关工作，做了一个原型，尝试了三条路线，排除了两个看似合理的解释，最后卡在一个很具体的瓶颈上。此时你问：“现在的现象同时支持 A 和 B，但已有实验无法区分它们。下一步做什么干预最有信息量？”这不再是请专家替你完成研究，而是在一个极窄、极关键的位置上调用他的判断。你的一百小时工作，加上他的十分钟洞察，可能让整个问题向前跨出一大步。

这并不是要求人在求助前做到完美，更不是把独自硬撑当作美德。重点在于，先把自己能消除的不确定性尽量消除，再把真正剩下的部分说清楚。高质量的求助应该具体、有限，而且恰好落在对方最有比较优势的地方。真正好的模式既不是永远独立，也不是把问题一开始就交出去，而是先让事情产生运动，再在最需要的节点上寻求杠杆。

传播不是自我营销，而是信息路由

不过，只顾埋头做事也可能走向另一个极端。很多 Builder 都喜欢相信：只要东西足够好，正确的人迟早会发现它。现实通常没有这么浪漫。创造价值和让价值被发现，是两个不同的问题。一个优秀的开源项目可能一直躺在只有三个 Star 的仓库里，一套真正有用的 Benchmark 也可能因为没有进入相关研究者的注意力范围而无人使用。价值已经存在，并不等于价值完成了传播。

所以 Distribution 本身也是工作的一部分。但这里追求的不是 Maximum Exposure，而是 Maximum Relevant Exposure：不是让尽可能多的人看见，而是让真正面对这个问题的人能够及时发现它。一万次随机浏览，可能不如五个正在研究同一瓶颈的人认真看一遍。一个发在正确研究群里的链接、朋友对相关同行的一次推荐，或者一封写给真正潜在使用者的具体邮件，都可能成为最初那条有效的边。

这会直接改变你联系别人的方式。“老师您好，我很喜欢您的工作，希望有机会认识”是在请求一段关系，却把创造谈话内容的责任留给了对方；“我做了一个与你最近论文里某类失败直接相关的 Benchmark，其中一个结果让我重新思考了你们的解释”则是在传递可能有用的信息。前者索取注意力，后者路由价值。即使最终没有形成合作，后者仍然可能是一次值得发生的交流。

新项目最初往往需要这种主动的 Network Seeding。在围绕一个想法的网络出现之前，总要有人先建立最早的几条连接。你把项目发给少数真正受这个问题困扰的人，有人试用，有人指出漏洞，有人把它转给同事，还有人开了 Issue 或提出新的实验。最开始，是你把项目推向人；如果它确实解决了问题，方向会逐渐反过来，人开始主动找到项目，也开始把更多人带到项目周围。

当这种变化发生时，项目就不再只是一个输出，它开始成为一个“协调吸引子”：原本分散的注意力、能力和行动，因为一个共同对象而汇聚起来。Benchmark 给不同团队提供同一个测量目标，开源项目给陌生人提供可以共同动手的表面，一个足够重要的科学问题甚至能够让几代研究者持续投入。它们真正有力量的地方，不只是吸引眼球，而是让人们有理由彼此发生行动关系。

这也提供了一种比普通 networking 更有野心的策略。与其问“我怎样才能认识更多厉害的人”，不如问“我能不能创造一个厉害的人也愿意参与的东西”。一个个维护关系时，你始终是每条边的中心，所有连接都依赖你主动发起和刷新；当一个值得协作的对象出现，网络结构会发生变化。项目成为见面的地方，问题成为共同语言，人们通过作品发现彼此，也通过作品认识你。

从信任种子到能力地图

两个陌生人第一次进行高质量交流后，真正留下来的并不只是“聊过一次”。对方脑中会开始形成一个关于你的压缩模型：这个人在研究什么，对哪些问题有判断，做事是否扎实，交流后能不能产生进展。这些信息最初可能很少，但已经足够成为一颗信任种子。以后当相关问题再次出现时，记忆会把问题和人连接起来：遇到评估问题，会想到那个真正研究过评估的人；项目需要某种能力，会想到已经展示过这种能力的人。

所以关系真正建立的标志，不是加了微信，也不是彼此记得名字，而是进入了对方的 capability map。对方知道你擅长什么，知道什么问题可以来找你，也大致知道把一件事交给你会发生什么。随着一次次靠谱的互动，这个模型会继续更新：“我见过这个人”变成“这个问题可以问他”，再变成“这部分工作可以交给他”，最后可能变成“如果遇到合适的机会，我应该想到他”。

介绍之所以有价值，也是因为它并不只是提供入口，而是在转移信任。一个人把你介绍给他的合作者，实际上是在拿出一小部分自己的信誉，为“这次连接值得发生”作担保。这样的担保不可能凭空产生，它通常来自共同做过的事情。真实协作会暴露大量平时看不到的信息：一个人如何面对模糊，怎样处理失败，是否守住承诺，能不能清楚表达限制，又是否愿意在证据改变时修正自己的判断。

从这个角度看，真正成熟的关系网络并不是一份联系人名单，而是一个分布式的能力与信任索引。谁真正理解这个问题？谁在这里有好的判断？谁能在不确定中推进工作？一个新机会出现时应该想到谁？网络的价值，不在于里面有多少节点，而在于这些节点能否准确地理解彼此，让问题、能力和机会以更低的成本找到正确的人。

因此，一种很重要的社会资本并不是“很多人知道我”，而是“正确的人准确地知道我擅长什么”。你不需要反复描述自己，直到某个标签被人记住。更可靠的方式，是留下足够多、一致而可验证的证据，让别人自然形成那个判断。被广泛认识未必有用，被正确索引才真正改变机会的流向。

关系发生在最后

所以，这篇文章并不是在说“不要社交”，而是在说：不要把社交动作误认为真实进展。去做一件值得别人因此认识你的事，把能力变成别人能够检查的证据；先独立推进，再在真正需要的地方请求帮助；把做出的价值送到最相关的人面前，让共同的问题产生交流，让交流留下证据，让证据逐渐变成信任。

不要为了得到关系而刻意制造谈话，而要在推进真实问题时，让关系自然发生。也不要只想着怎样接近厉害的人，试着创造一个厉害的人也愿意加入的东西。最有力量的网络，往往不是被一个人直接“搭建”出来的，而是从一项让人们有理由彼此找到的工作周围生长出来的。

创造价值，让它能够被发现，再给人们一个可以共同协作的表面。关系发生在最后。
entry.summary: 关于作品、信任与连接：有价值的关系，往往是在共同推进真实问题的过程中长出来的。

entry.title: The Network Comes Later
entry.content:
中文

TL;DR — Meaningful professional relationships are not built by pursuing access to people. They emerge when shared problems make ability visible, useful work reaches the right people, and repeated evidence compounds into trust. Build something worth coordinating around; the network comes later.

I have become increasingly suspicious of the way people talk about networking. The usual advice begins with a list of people: Who should I meet? Who matters in this field? How can I get introduced? What should I say so that they remember me? Once those questions become the starting point, it is easy to fall into a familiar pattern—adding someone on WeChat after a conference, sending a respected researcher a vague note about “learning from them,” or asking for collaboration before there is anything concrete to collaborate on. The exchange may be polite, but it contains almost no information. The other person still does not know what you care about, what you can do, how you think, or whether working with you would move anything forward. You have requested a relationship before giving that relationship a reason to exist.

My instinct now is almost the opposite: do not begin with the relationship. Begin with something real. Begin with a problem you are willing to work on, a claim you are willing to test, a tool you are willing to build, or a question that can survive contact with evidence. Meaningful professional relationships tend to appear downstream of those commitments. The strongest ones are rarely built by two people staring at each other and trying to manufacture affinity. They are built by two people looking in the same direction, noticing the same part of the world, and discovering that each has something useful to contribute to the other’s understanding of it.

Shared reality before connection

Imagine two researchers studying long-running agents. One believes the central bottleneck is memory; the other believes it is evaluation. They do not need to agree in order to have a meaningful relationship. Their disagreement already has structure because both are responding to the same object. They can compare evidence, expose assumptions, design interventions, and learn from the places where their models diverge. The conversation does not need an artificial opening line, because the problem itself generates the conversation. What begins as “I want to know this person” is replaced by something more grounded: “We are both trying to understand this thing.” That shift is small in language but enormous in consequence.

This is why serious intellectual communities often form around questions rather than personalities. Researchers recognize one another while repeatedly colliding with the same bottleneck. Builders begin exchanging tools because their problems touch. People with different beliefs about the same phenomenon argue, collaborate, and gradually sharpen one another’s thinking. The relationship becomes a by-product of sustained attention to shared reality. It is not a prize granted before the work begins, and it is not a separate social layer floating above the work. It is part of the coordination that becomes necessary once multiple people care enough about the same thing to act on it.

None of this means that every human interaction should become instrumental, or that friendship and curiosity require a measurable output. That would reproduce the same mistake in a colder form. The point is not “never talk to people.” It is to avoid manufactured networking: pursuing contact as if contact itself were progress, treating people as resources, or attempting to create intimacy without shared substance. A better principle is to spend less energy asking how to know a particular person and more energy asking what you could work on that would give both of you a natural reason to speak.

Proof before proximity

The difficulty is that ability is invisible until it leaves evidence. You may believe that you understand agents, benchmarks, or research methodology; you may believe that you have unusual taste or the capacity to do difficult work. But all of this is latent. From the outside, potential cannot be inspected directly. Other people can only update their model of you through what becomes observable: the code you write, the experiments you run, the failures you identify, the essays you publish, the questions you formulate, and the way you respond when the first approach does not work.

A repository, benchmark, dataset, pull request, careful analysis, or surprising negative result is therefore more than an output. It is evidence. Each piece of work converts an uncheckable claim about ability into something another person can examine. Repeated evidence makes competence legible. It allows people to infer what kinds of problems you notice, whether you distinguish confidence from speculation, whether you finish what you start, and whether interacting with you tends to move a problem forward. Trust does not emerge from how confidently you describe yourself. It emerges as other people accumulate reasons to believe that your judgment and execution are reliable.

This is why ten hours spent making something real can be more socially valuable than ten hours spent trying to meet people. Good work speaks on your behalf, but more importantly, it lowers the cost of understanding you. Instead of asking someone to imagine what you might be capable of, you give them an object through which they can see how you think. The interaction changes from “Please give me some of your attention” to “I have already moved this problem forward; here is what I found, and here is the part that remains unresolved.” You are no longer requesting proximity in the hope that value might later appear. You are bringing evidence of value into the conversation from the beginning.

The same logic explains why doing most of the work yourself is such a strong signal. It shows that you are not waiting for another person to supply momentum. If someone offers you a useful idea, an introduction, or ten minutes of expert judgment, there is evidence that you can absorb that leverage and multiply it. This makes helping you less like adopting an unfinished obligation and more like placing a small amount of force at a point where the system is already moving.

Ask after doing the work

Asking for help too early often produces weak interactions because the request quietly transfers most of the cognitive burden to the other person. A question like “How should I pursue this research direction?” requires the expert to define the problem, map the search space, generate hypotheses, and decide what you should do next. The apparent humility of the question conceals how much work it demands. In contrast, suppose you have read the relevant literature, built a prototype, tried three approaches, eliminated two explanations, and isolated the uncertainty that remains. You can now ask: “The evidence is consistent with A or B, but my current experiment cannot distinguish them. What intervention would be most informative?” That is a completely different object.

At that point, the expert is not being asked to perform your work. They are applying a small amount of specialized judgment precisely where their comparative advantage is greatest. A hundred hours of independent effort can be unlocked by ten minutes of insight. The exchange is valuable to you, but it is also easier and more interesting for the other person because they are responding to a developed problem rather than an empty space. The result is not merely an answer. It is evidence that you know how to formulate uncertainty, respect another person’s time, and turn advice into progress.

This does not mean waiting until the work is perfect or refusing help as a matter of pride. The goal is to reduce uncertainty as far as you reasonably can, state clearly what you have tried, and expose the actual bottleneck. High-quality help becomes possible when the request is concrete, bounded, and directed toward something the other person is unusually equipped to see. The best pattern is not independence forever. It is independent motion followed by precise coordination.

Distribution is part of the work

There is an opposite romantic error among builders: the belief that if the work is good enough, the right people will inevitably discover it. Often they will not. Value creation and value discovery are different problems. An excellent project can remain invisible in a repository with three stars; a useful benchmark can fail to reach the teams who need it; an important idea can disappear because it never entered the channels through which relevant people allocate attention. Building is necessary, but the existence of value does not guarantee its discovery.

Distribution must therefore be treated as part of the work. In this context, distribution is not self-promotion and should not be optimized for maximum exposure. It is an information-routing problem: what have I created, who would genuinely find it useful, and through which trusted channels can it reach them? Five views from researchers actively working on the same bottleneck may be worth more than ten thousand random impressions. A message in the right research group, a link sent to one builder with an adjacent problem, or a recommendation from a trusted colleague may be enough to create the first meaningful edge.

This changes how outreach is written. “I admire your work and would love to connect” requests a relationship while offering little evidence about why the interaction should continue. “I built a benchmark related to the failure mode in your recent paper, and one result made me reconsider your explanation” does something else: it routes potentially relevant value. The first message asks the recipient to invent the substance of the exchange. The second arrives with a shared object already in view. Even if no relationship follows, the interaction can still be worthwhile because the information itself has a reason to travel.

Early work often needs this kind of deliberate network seeding. Before a community exists around an idea, someone must create the first edges. You show the work to a small number of people who genuinely face the problem. One person tries it, another identifies a flaw, a third forwards it to a colleague, and someone else opens an issue or proposes an extension. At first, you are pushing the work toward people. If the object proves useful, the direction gradually reverses: people begin finding the work, bringing in other people, and creating connections that no longer depend on your direct effort.

At that point, the work begins to function as a coordination attractor—something that concentrates attention, ability, and action that would otherwise remain scattered. A benchmark gives different research groups a common measurement target. An open-source project gives strangers a shared surface on which to contribute. A serious scientific question can organize communities for decades, even when many of the participants never meet. The attractor matters not merely because it is interesting, but because it gives people a reason to act in relation to one another.

This suggests a more ambitious alternative to ordinary networking. Instead of asking, “How can I meet more impressive people?” ask, “What could I create that thoughtful people would naturally want to engage with?” Building relationships one by one keeps you at the center of every edge; each connection must be initiated, maintained, and refreshed. Creating an object worth coordinating around changes the topology. The project becomes a meeting place, the question becomes a shared language, and people begin discovering the work, one another, and eventually you through the work itself.

From a trust seed to a capability map

When two strangers have one serious exchange, the most important result is not that they have spoken once. It is that each person begins forming a compressed model of the other. The model may initially contain only a few facts: what this person works on, what they appear to understand, whether their judgment was useful, and whether they followed through. Those facts are enough to plant a trust seed. Later, when a related problem appears, the person may be retrieved from memory. An evaluation question appears, and you remember the person who thinks clearly about evaluation. A project needs a particular skill, and you remember who has already demonstrated it.

This is a deeper threshold than exchanging contact details. A relationship begins to matter when each person enters the other’s capability map—when both have an accurate enough model of what the other is good for, where their judgment is reliable, and when involving them would improve the work. Repeated interactions sharpen that model. “I have met this person” becomes “I can ask this person about this topic.” Later it becomes “I would trust this person with this part of the work.” Eventually it may become “If I see the right opportunity, I should bring this person in.”

Introductions have value for exactly this reason. A strong introduction is not simply access to someone else’s attention; it is transferred trust. The person making the introduction spends a small amount of their own reputation on the claim that the connection is worth making. That claim becomes credible when it is grounded in evidence, especially evidence produced through shared work. Working together reveals far more than a polished self-description ever could: how someone behaves under ambiguity, responds to failure, communicates constraints, keeps commitments, and changes their mind when the evidence changes.

Over time, a real network becomes much more than a collection of contacts. It becomes a distributed index of capability and trust. Who understands this problem? Who has good judgment here? Who can execute under uncertainty? Who should be invited into this opportunity? A mature network answers these questions continuously, routing new problems and opportunities toward people who have become legible through prior action. Its value lies less in how many nodes it contains than in how accurately those nodes understand one another.

One of the most important forms of social capital, then, is not being widely known. It is being correctly indexed. You want the right people to have an accurate model of what you are unusually good at. The cleanest way to create that model is not to repeat a description of yourself until it becomes familiar. It is to leave enough evidence that the description becomes unnecessary.

The network comes later

The argument is not “do not socialize.” It is “do not mistake social motion for meaningful progress.” Work on things worth knowing you for. Make your ability legible through evidence. Push a problem as far as you can before asking for leverage. Route what you create toward the people for whom it is genuinely relevant. Let shared problems generate conversations, let useful interactions generate trust, and let trust route future collaborations, introductions, and opportunities.

Do not create conversations merely to acquire relationships. Let relationships emerge while advancing problems that matter. And instead of spending all your energy trying to meet impressive people, create something that impressive people would have a reason to join. The strongest network is often not the one you assemble directly. It is the one that forms around work that gives people a reason to find one another.

Create value. Make it discoverable. Give people a surface on which to coordinate. The network comes later.
